extracted.intended_audience: readers of the Philosophical Transactions / experimental natural philosophers (Fellows of the Royal Society) and observational astronomers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit evaluative criteria for conducting, reporting, and judging experimental and observational natural-philosophy work (particularly optics, astronomy, mineralogy, and chemical/metal experiments) as exemplified in 17th‑century Philosophical Transactions letters and reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of illumination and source when doing prism/spectrum experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the coloured spectrum observed from a prism is produced by true sun‑beams (a point source) rather than rays from a bright cloud or extended luminous source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer notes that a spectrum appearing much longer than broad can result when the sun is behind a white cloud (an extended source) or when the hole is large enough to enlighten the whole prism; to reproduce Newton's experiment reliably one must use clear skies or identify whether the illuminating source is the true sun or an illuminated cloud. Mere change in source size/quality explains apparent departures from 'received laws of refraction.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prism placement relative to aperture to avoid divergence artefacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the prism close to the aperture (the little hole in the window) so the light has no room to diverge and the coloured image appears transverse rather than parallel to the prism axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton's reply emphasizes that the experiment as represented was tried in clear days with the prism placed close to the hole; improper placement or allowing divergence can alter the spectrum's form and lead to incorrect theoretical conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experimental replication and experience to confirm interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Give weight to repeated empirical trials and demonstrations: verify phenomena by independent repetition and by showing experiments to knowledgeable observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Francis Linus appeals to 'mere experience' and to demonstrations shown long before to Kenelm Digby; the text treats reproduction and demonstration to peers as substantive confirmation of observational claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify instrument accuracy targets when designing astronomical instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: State the intended measurement precision (e.g., show the moon's true place to a minute or two; give semi‑diameters and parallaxes to a second).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamsteed contrasts instruments that cannot show the true place to half a degree with his proposed contrivance designed to show lunar longitude to a minute or two and provide semi‑diameters and parallaxes to a second; explicit accuracy goals inform instrument design and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for atmospheric refraction at higher altitudes in solar tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Include refraction corrections for solar altitudes above 30 degrees when constructing solar motion/numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamsteed notes he had neglected to apply refractions above 30° in earlier numbers and that reason and experience show they are not insensible; correcting for these refractions led him to make new solar numbers more consistent with Cassini's observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer more accurate observational sources and reconcile conflicting tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare candidate observational corpora (e.g., Cassini vs Tycho) and prefer the more accurate set when deriving astronomical constants; reconcile differences by targeted recalculation and testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamsteed found Cassini's observations more accurate than Tycho's and sought numbers to match them; this included promoting the apogee and recalculating the greatest equation to better fit observed phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test refraction tables by examining day‑time observations of stars near the Sun
rubrics_metrics.description: Use skilful examination of daytime observations of star distances from the sun (observed preceding/following nights) to determine the true magnitude of solar equation and test the correctness of refraction entries in tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamsteed presents an expedient: examine observations of distances of stars by day (and corresponding night observations) and apply refraction considerations to deduce differences between mean and equal motion and the greatest equation of the sun's orb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct solar position before deriving planetary motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before attempting to represent planetary motions by numbers, correct the sun's position and motions because errors in the sun's place propagate into planetary position errors (e.g., errors of several hours in opposition timing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamsteed argues Tycho's large equation produced significant errors in planetary observations taken at opposition; therefore planetary corrections must follow solar corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report observational timings with comparable references and clocks
rubrics_metrics.description: Record immersion/emersion and shadow times precisely, document instruments used (e.g., pendulum clocks) and present observed times alongside predictions from tables for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The eclipse account gives observed times at locations (Derby, London, Paris), lists times by pendulum clock, and compares them to Flamsteed's tables; this side‑by‑side reporting is required to evaluate observation accuracy and timing differences (also to infer longitude differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geographically distributed simultaneous observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain observations from multiple locations (different longitudes) to measure timing differences and improve positional determinations (e.g., Derby vs London vs Paris).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The eclipse report contrasts Derby and London observations (longitude difference ~5 minutes) and includes Paris data, showing the practice of using multiple stations to triangulate and validate event timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document experimental procedure, reagents, and observable outcomes in chemical/metal experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing a metallurgical or chemical process (e.g., vitrifying antimony), specify reagent quantities, preparatory steps, heating state, actions (fluxing, adding cauk-stone), and observable results (yield, appearance, whether reagents incorporate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lister gives a recipe: one pound antimony, flux clear, add ounce or two of red‑hot cauk‑stone, flux a few minutes, cast and decant; notes yield (~15 ounces vitrum), appearance (like polished steel), and that cauk does not incorporate—these details enable reproducibility and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record provenance, locality, and descriptive morphology for mineral/crystal observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe where specimens were found, their size, form (planes, columns), colour, surface features (rugged adhesion, embossed work), and associated rock context to support identification and comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the descriptions of odd‑figured iris and glossopetrae, the author records localities (e.g., Hinderskelf‑park, Sheppey), sizes (wheat‑corn to hundred times larger), number and arrangement of planes, colours, and adherence—essential for mineralogical taxonomy and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple qualitative tests and repeated observation to distinguish mineral types
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply taste, solubility behaviour, reactions with reagents (e.g., gall to test for purple tincture), exposure effects (cellar vs sun), and reappearance after wiping to characterize efflorescences and distinguish mineral kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lister compares aluminous versus vitriolic fibres by taste (alumy vs styptic), solubility (ebullition vs quiet dissolution), reaction with gall (vitriolic gives purple), and behaviour when exposed in cellar or window—these empirical checks support identification claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer biological reproductive structures by careful morphological and functional analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: To argue that a fungus has flowers and seeds, examine gill structure, separability when ripe, seed impressions in the head, arrangement (spiral), and test viability (sowing) and staining/colour changes on cutting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lister compares mushroom gills to artichoke seed arrangement, notes seeds are distinct and leave impressions, observes immediate colour changes when cut and juice staining properties, and acknowledges steril seed cases—these observations form the basis for asserting fungal reproductive anatomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: When writing accounts or reviews of scientific books, summarise contents, methods, and contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an outline of the book's parts, list major topics and methods (e.g., experiments tried, mathematical contents), note novelties or useful treatises, and highlight where the work contributes to current knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Account of some Books' sections summarize tract contents (e.g., Boyle's tracts on air qualities, preservation in vacuo, critique of Hobbes), list experiments and subjects, and assess usefulness—serving as a model for critical bibliographic reporting.
